document.title: Event Management Platform Architecture
document.subtitle: C4 views of the Event Management Platform for **architects and new engineers**: context, containers, components and six runtime flows. Written by hand from the repository at commit `4625169`; no Lantern output.

revisions.author: Independent second pass
revisions.summary: Verified against the code: the gateway rate limiter fails open, not closed; filter order and scan outcomes corrected; three Low risks and two JWKS callers added. See verification.md.

p-attendee.name: Attendee
p-attendee.description: Registers, signs in, books tickets, pays, sees their tickets and payments, asks for refunds and sets notification preferences; receives booking, payment, ticket and reminder messages.

properties.access: Role ATTENDEE, granted to every self-registered account

p-organizer.name: Organizer
p-organizer.description: Manages their own venues and rooms, creates events and ticket types, publishes, opens sales, cancels or completes events, refunds bookings of their events and scans tickets at their events.

p-staff.name: Event staff
p-staff.description: Validates QR tickets and checks attendees in at the door.

properties.access: Role EVENT_STAFF, assigned by an administrator; may scan tickets of any event

p-admin.name: Administrator
p-admin.description: Assigns roles, reads the security audit log, manages event categories, acts on any event, venue or payment, and inspects locally recorded email and SMS output.

properties.access: Role ADMIN; bootstrapped from configuration, disabled by default

emp.name: Event Management Platform
emp.description: Lets organizers publish events in their venues and sell tickets, and lets attendees book, pay for, receive and use QR tickets, with refunds and notifications.

oauth-idp.name: OAuth2 identity provider
oauth-idp.description: Optional social or corporate login through Spring Security client registration; must supply a verified email. Switched off by default and no provider is configured in the repository.

gateway.name: api-gateway
gateway.description: The public entry point: validates the JWT on protected routes, strips client identity headers, enforces CORS and correlation ids, rate-limits sign-up, login and refresh in Redis, and routes by path to fixed service URLs.

properties.stack: Spring Cloud 2025.0.2 gateway (WebFlux), OAuth2 resource server, reactive Redis, springdoc

auth.name: auth-service
auth.description: Identity: accounts with BCrypt passwords, RS256 access tokens and their public JWKS, rotating refresh sessions, roles, optional OAuth2 login and a security audit log.

properties.stack: Spring Security, OAuth2 resource server and client, Spring Data JPA, Flyway

event.name: event-service
event.description: Event lifecycle, categories, ticket types and authoritative ticket inventory with locked holds; public event discovery cached in Redis; reserves rooms at venue-service; publishes event and inventory events.

venue.name: venue-service

properties.stack: Spring MVC, Spring Data JPA, Flyway

attendee.name: attendee-service

payment.name: payment-service
payment.description: Payments, attempts, transactions, refunds, signed provider webhooks and reconciliation behind a provider port; the only provider is an in-process fake.

properties.stack: Spring MVC, Spring Data JPA, Spring Kafka, Flyway

notification.name: notification-service
notification.description: Turns lifecycle events into durable email and SMS intents with preferences, templates, retries and reminders; the only senders record the message locally instead of sending it.

properties.stack: Spring MVC, Spring Data JPA, Spring Kafka, Flyway

redis.name: Redis
redis.description: Gateway rate-limit buckets for sign-up, login and refresh, and event-service's public event detail cache (TTL 5 min).

auth-db.name: auth_service

event-db.name: event_service

venue-db.name: venue_service

attendee-db.name: attendee_service

t-event.name: event-platform.event-lifecycle.v1
t-event.description: Event lifecycle (published, updated, cancelled), ticket-type changes and inventory facts (held, confirmed, released, expired, confirmation or release rejected).

t-attendee.name: event-platform.attendee-lifecycle.v1
t-attendee.description: Booking facts (created, payment requested, confirmed, payment failed, refunded), hold expiry, ticket issued and checked in, and the Saga commands for inventory confirmation or release and payment compensation.

t-payment.name: event-platform.payment-lifecycle.v1
t-payment.description: Payment processing, succeeded and failed; refund succeeded and failed.

gw-edge.name: Edge filters
gw-edge.description: Sets or validates X-Correlation-Id, rejects origins not on the allow-list, removes client-sent X-User-* identity headers and adds security headers.

gw-rate-limit.name: Authentication rate limiter
gw-rate-limit.description: Limits POST register, login and refresh per client IP; answers 429 when exceeded. If Redis fails, Spring Cloud Gateway's RedisRateLimiter lets the request through (fails open).

gw-security.name: JWT security chain
gw-security.description: Lets public routes through and requires a valid RS256 access token (issuer, audience, typ=access) on every other /api/v1 path; keys come from auth-service's JWKS.

gw-routes.name: Route table
gw-routes.description: Forwards by path prefix to fixed service URLs, keeping the original bearer token.

au-api.name: Auth API
au-api.description: Register, login, refresh, logout, revoke all sessions, current user, role replacement (ADMIN) and audit log (ADMIN).

au-jwks.name: JWKS endpoint and key material
au-jwks.description: Publishes the current RSA public key; loads the key pair from PEM files or generates an ephemeral 2048-bit key at startup.

au-authn.name: Authentication service
au-authn.technology: Spring service · BCrypt · Nimbus JWT encoder
au-authn.description: Checks passwords, issues 10-minute RS256 access tokens, rotates opaque refresh tokens under a row lock and revokes the family on reuse.

au-oauth.name: OAuth2 login
au-oauth.description: When enabled, completes a provider login, requires a verified email, creates or finds the linked account and returns the token pair as JSON.

au-audit.name: Security audit
au-audit.description: Records every registration, login, refresh, revocation and role change with request metadata.

ev-public.name: Public discovery
ev-public.description: Lists events and categories and serves event details without a token; details are cached in Redis.

ev-manage.name: Event management
ev-manage.description: Organizer and admin commands: create and update drafts, ticket types, transitions (publish, open sales, sold out, cancel, complete) and archive.

ev-inventory.name: Inventory
ev-inventory.description: Idempotent hold, confirm and release on locked ticket rows; holds expire after 15 minutes.

ev-venue-client.name: Venue client
ev-venue-client.description: Reserves and releases the room at venue-service with the organizer's bearer token.

ev-saga.name: Inventory Saga consumer
ev-saga.description: Executes inventory confirmation and release commands from attendee-service; turns business errors into rejection events.

ev-outbox.name: Event outbox
ev-outbox.description: Writes event records in the business transaction and relays them every second; dead-letters a row after 10 failed attempts.

ve-api.name: Venue API
ve-api.description: Venue, room and availability-block management for owning organizers and admins.

ve-availability.name: Availability and reservations
ve-availability.description: Checks availability and reserves or releases a venue or room for an owner reference, under a lock on the venue row.

ve-location.name: Location enrichment
ve-location.description: Placeholder for geocoding: returns the supplied coordinates unchanged.

at-booking.name: Booking API
at-booking.description: Creates bookings from a durable idempotent command, lists bookings and tickets, and keeps the attendee profile.

at-event-client.name: Event inventory client
at-event-client.description: Holds and, for free tickets, confirms inventory at event-service with the attendee's bearer token and stable keys.

at-saga.name: Booking Saga
at-saga.description: Moves each booking through payment, inventory confirmation, ticket issue, expiry, compensation and refund; recovers stuck Sagas every 5 s and expires holds every 30 s.

at-consumers.name: Lifecycle consumers
at-consumers.description: Feed inventory, event-cancellation and payment events into the Saga, deduplicated by message id.

at-scan.name: Ticket scanning
at-scan.description: Signs QR tokens; validates them and checks tickets in exactly once under a row lock, auditing every scan.

at-outbox.name: Attendee outbox
at-outbox.description: Relays booking, ticket and Saga-command records to the attendee topic every second.

pa-api.name: Payment API
pa-api.description: Pay for a booking, list and read payments and their transactions, verify, refund, and receive signed provider webhooks.

pa-payments.name: Payment processing
pa-payments.description: Claims a payment for a projected booking order, calls the provider outside the transaction, applies the result, deduplicates webhooks and reconciles stuck PROCESSING payments every 10 s.

pa-refunds.name: Refunds
pa-refunds.description: Full or partial refunds for the attendee, the event's organizer or an admin until the event starts, and full compensation refunds for the Saga.

pa-provider.name: Fake payment provider
pa-provider.description: Deterministic sandbox outcomes chosen by token, payment state held in memory, HMAC webhook signatures; no network call.

pa-consumer.name: Attendee events consumer
pa-consumer.description: Builds the booking payment order and ticket projections and runs compensation refunds.

pa-outbox.name: Payment outbox
pa-outbox.description: Relays payment and refund records to the payment topic every second.

no-api.name: Notification API
no-api.description: Reads and updates the caller's preferences, lists their notifications and, for admins, the locally recorded deliveries.

no-planner.name: Event handler and planner
no-planner.description: Consumes the three lifecycle topics, keeps recipient and booking projections and plans one idempotent intent per message, recipient and channel, including reminders 24 h before the start.

no-delivery.name: Delivery job
no-delivery.description: Every second locks due intents, renders the template and calls the email or SMS port; retries up to 5 times, then dead-letters.

no-local.name: Local email and SMS adapters
no-local.description: Store the rendered message in local_deliveries instead of sending it; the only implementations.

pages.title: Event Management Platform
pages.summary: The Event Management Platform sells tickets for events held in organizers' own venues: organizers publish events and open sales, attendees book and pay, staff check them in with signed QR tickets. The most important fact for anyone changing it: **bookings are a Kafka-driven Saga across attendee-, event- and payment-service**, so most state changes arrive asynchronously through transactional outboxes.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
This document is for **architects and new engineers**. It was written by hand from the code of the `Event-Management-platform` repository at commit `4625169` (2026-08-16), on 2026-10-29. Lantern produced none of it.

The repository records its decisions as nine ADRs; they are summarised at the end of this page and checked against the code. Owners and quality goals are not recorded. All payment, email and SMS providers are local stand-ins, so the system has no real outside dependency yet; people reach it through the HTTP API, because the web front end is only a landing page.

sections.body: Left out on purpose. **Payment, email and SMS providers** are ports with only local implementations: payments go to an in-process fake and messages are stored in notification-service's database, so no outside system receives them. The maps provider is a no-op adapter. Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Jaeger and the OpenTelemetry collector only observe the system, and GitHub Actions only builds it.

pages.title: Requests and data
pages.summary: The synchronous view: who calls the gateway, where it routes, which service calls which over HTTP, and which store each service owns.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
All public traffic is meant to enter through **api-gateway** on port 8080. The gateway checks the token on protected routes and forwards the original bearer token; **every service validates it again** against auth-service's JWKS and enforces roles and ownership itself. Only two service-to-service HTTP calls exist, both carrying the end user's token: event-service → venue-service (room reservation) and attendee-service → event-service (inventory holds). Everything else between services goes through Kafka (next page).

The `shared/` modules (Kafka reliability, web error handling, header contracts) are libraries compiled into the services, not containers.

pages.title: Messaging
pages.summary: The asynchronous view: three Kafka topics, each written by one service through its transactional outbox, carry the booking Saga, ticket facts and everything notification-service turns into messages.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body: Each producing service writes an outbox row in the same transaction as its change; a relay publishes due rows every second, keyed by aggregate id, with standard headers (`messageId`, `eventType`, `schemaVersion`, correlation and trace). After 10 failed sends a row is kept as dead-lettered. Consumers store each processed `messageId` in the same transaction as their effect; failures are retried four times with exponential backoff and then go to `<topic>.dlt`, which nothing consumes. auth-service and venue-service use no Kafka.

pages.title: Cancel an event
pages.summary: An organizer cancels a published or on-sale event. event-service releases the room at venue-service and records `event.cancelled`. attendee-service cancels the event's bookings and tickets, and notification-service cancels reminders and alerts each attendee. **No refund is started**: paid attendees must ask for one before the original start time.

sections.title: Recorded decisions
sections.body: The decisions below come from `docs/adr/` (all *Accepted*), followed by decisions seen only in code and configuration, whose rationale is *not recorded*. Each was checked against the code; where the code differs the risk table says so.

items.title: Kafka is the only message broker
items.body: Versioned event schemas, at-least-once delivery, correlation and trace context in headers. Holds in code: three lifecycle topics, no other broker.

items.title: Database per service
items.body: Six PostgreSQL databases, one login each with CONNECT revoked from PUBLIC; locally all in one PostgreSQL container (`docker/postgres/init-databases.sql`).

items.title: Orchestrated Saga with transactional outboxes
items.body: attendee-service orchestrates; event-, attendee- and payment-service publish only through their outbox tables; no XA.

items.title: RS256 access tokens checked at every boundary, rotated refresh sessions
items.body: The gateway and each service validate the token against auth-service's JWKS; refresh tokens are opaque, hashed and rotated, reuse revokes the family. Access tokens are not revoked before expiry (10 minutes).

items.title: Locked inventory holds and venue reservation over HTTP
items.body: Ticket rows are locked for every hold change; publication reserves the room through venue-service with the organizer's token and owner reference `event:<id>`.

items.title: Durable booking commands, signed QR tickets, locked check-in
items.body: A booking command row is claimed before calling event-service; QR tokens are HMAC-SHA256 signed; check-in locks the ticket row.

items.title: Provider-neutral payments with a fake adapter; recoverable Saga
items.body: One provider port; only a deterministic fake exists. Refund policy by role; stuck payments and Saga steps are re-driven by scheduled jobs.

items.title: Bounded Kafka retries and durable notification delivery
items.body: Four exponential retries then `<topic>.dlt`; outbox rows dead-lettered after 10 attempts; notifications stored as intents with attempts.

items.title: Fixed service URLs, no service discovery
items.body: The gateway and the two HTTP clients use configured URLs (`http://<service>:<port>` in compose). Rationale: not recorded.

items.title: Redis for auth rate limits and the public event cache
items.body: One Redis serves the gateway's rate limiter and event-service's Spring cache. Rationale: not recorded (system-context.md allows Redis for caches and rate limits).

items.title: One repository, one Maven reactor, one backend Dockerfile
items.body: All services build from `docker/backend.Dockerfile` with a `MODULE` argument; shared libraries hold no domain code. Rationale: not recorded.

sections.title: Risks and findings
rows: event-service's inventory endpoints are reachable through the gateway by any attendee: the gateway routes all of `/api/v1/events/**` and only requires a token, and the endpoints allow the ATTENDEE role. An attendee can hold seats and confirm their own hold without a booking or payment.
Seats can be taken out of sale permanently without paying; repeated holds can also block sales for 15 minutes at a time.

Cancelling an event cancels its bookings and tickets in attendee-service but requests no refund; no service reacts to `event.cancelled` with money. Refunds stay a manual call that closes when the event's start time passes.
Paid attendees of a cancelled event keep being charged unless someone refunds each payment before the original start time.

Default configuration is local-only: the JWT signing key and the QR signing key are generated at startup when none is configured (allowed by default), the payment webhook secret defaults to a known value, and all database passwords are `local_dev_only`.
Restarting auth-service logs everyone out; restarting attendee-service makes every issued QR ticket fail at the door; a deployment that keeps the defaults accepts forged webhooks.

Redis is on event-service's write path: business transactions evict the cache by calling `Cache.evict` directly, which no cache error handler covers, and cached detail reads use Spring's default handler, which rethrows.

A Redis outage makes event publication, transitions, inventory holds (so every booking) and public event details fail. (The gateway's login rate limiter does not block: it fails open, so the limits stop applying.)
Publishing and cancelling an event call venue-service over HTTP inside the event database transaction.

If the transaction rolls back after the call (e.g. Redis or database failure), the room stays reserved, or is released while the event stays published. The idempotent `event:<id>` reference only helps if publication is retried.

Personal data and ticket credentials travel through Kafka and are copied: `booking.created`, `ticket.issued` and payment events carry email, phone and locale, and `ticket.issued` carries the signed QR token, which notification-service stores in intent variables and local deliveries.
Anyone who can read the topics or notification_service can use other people's tickets; GDPR erasure has to reach three services and the topics.
Single points of failure in the only deployment: one Kafka node with replication factor 1 and auto-created topics, one PostgreSQL for all six databases, one Redis.
Losing any of them stops bookings; losing the Kafka volume loses undelivered Saga commands already marked published.
The payment provider is an in-process fake that keeps payment state in memory.
After a restart, reconciliation of a payment still PROCESSING finds no provider record and marks it failed.
Compensation refunds call the provider inside the Kafka consumer's database transaction.
With a real, slow provider the consumer holds locks and stalls its partition; failures retry and end in the DLT.
Any EVENT_STAFF user may validate and check in tickets for every event; staff are not tied to events.
A staff account of one organizer can check in (consume) tickets of another organizer's event.

Cancelling an event does not stop bookings still awaiting payment: payment-service never hears of the cancellation, event-service confirms an active hold without checking the event status, and attendee-service confirms a booking from any status.
An attendee who pays within the 15-minute hold after a cancellation gets a confirmed booking and valid tickets for the cancelled event, and is charged.

Reminders and cancellation alerts are not withdrawn for bookings that end without tickets: notification-service plans the 24 h reminder on `booking.created` for every unexpired booking and ignores `booking.payment-failed`, `ticket-hold.expired` and `booking.refunded`; `event.cancelled` alerts every booking it has seen.
Attendees whose booking failed, expired or was refunded still get a reminder and a cancellation message.
The gateway rate-limits by the TCP peer address and ignores `X-Forwarded-For`, while the frontend's nginx proxies `/api/` to it.
All users who reach the API through the frontend share one sign-up, login and refresh bucket, so a few failed logins block everyone; any future load balancer has the same effect.
Every service port (8081-8086) is published on the host next to the gateway.
Callers can bypass the gateway's CORS, correlation and rate limiting (tokens are still checked by each service).
Reschedule alerts cannot fire: event details can change only while an event is a draft, and bookings exist only once sales are open.
The EVENT_RESCHEDULED notification and template are dead code.
Setting the email or SMS provider to anything but `local` leaves no sender bean, since no other adapter exists.
Observability gaps: Grafana has a Loki data source but nothing ships logs to Loki.
Logs exist only in container output.

Documentation and UI are behind the code: the front end says "Phase 3" and that booking is deferred, and system-context.md says notification delivery is deferred and draws users going through the front end.
New engineers get a wrong picture of what runs.

sections.title: Glossary
rows: Seats of one ticket type set aside for 15 minutes by event-service while a booking is paid; confirmed, released or expired.
The booking/payment workflow that attendee-service drives over Kafka: payment, inventory confirmation, ticket issue, or compensation.
A full refund requested by attendee-service when a payment succeeds but the seats can no longer be confirmed.
A table row written in the same database transaction as the business change and published to Kafka later by a relay.
Dead-letter topic: `<topic>.dlt`, where a record goes after the consumer's retries are exhausted.
Client-supplied request header; the same key with the same input returns the original result.
JSON Web Token (the access token) and JSON Web Key Set (the published public key that verifies it).
RSA signature with SHA-256: auth-service signs with a private key, everyone else verifies with the public key.
One refresh token row; a family is the chain of rotations from one login, revoked together on reuse.
An HMAC-SHA256-signed string identifying a ticket and event, shown at the door.
Kafka running without ZooKeeper; here a single node acts as broker and controller.
OpenTelemetry protocol, used to send traces to the collector.
